- Detrimental: food poisoning, food intoxication, foodborne illness, and food spoilage, meaning food made unfit to eat by undesirable flavors, appearance or smell.
- Neutral: microbes that neither cause disease nor change the food. They are just there, and we eat them along with it.

cards.t: Microbes in bread making (baker's yeast and sourdough)
q: what do microbes do in bread making
what yeast is used to make bread
cards.x:
Microbes do three jobs in bread making.
- Leavening: they make the flour-based dough rise, mainly with carbon dioxide and other gases.
- Flavor and aroma: they produce organic acids and alcohols.
- Conditioning: microbial enzymes act on gluten to give the dough elasticity, making it pliable and workable.

The microbes involved are Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast), certain Clostridium species, and certain Lactobacillus species, such as Lactobacillus sanfrancisco in sourdough.

cards.t: Beer and wine: alcoholic fermentation by yeast
q: what is the equation for alcoholic fermentation
what are the steps of brewing beer
cards.x:
Beer and wine come from alcoholic fermentation: yeast turns glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. One molecule of glucose yields 2 molecules of ethanol and 2 of carbon dioxide.

Beer brewing goes back to 6000 BCE (before the common era) in Sumeria, Egypt and Babylon. Its steps are malting the starch source, mashing, adding hops to the wort, lagering and filtration. Wine usually starts with grapes, but other fruit and plant material can be used, such as apples, oranges, pineapples, peaches and plums. Sometimes the yeast for an alcoholic drink comes from human saliva: the plant material is chewed (masticated) before brewing.

cards.t: Pickling, soy sauce and other fermented foods
q: what foods are made by fermentation
how are soy sauce and tofu made
cards.x:
Pickling preserves vegetable material in a salt brine; lactic acid may also be present, along with vinegar and spices. Cucumbers, cabbage, olives, okra, onions, ginger root and many more can be pickled.

Fermentation also turns soybeans and their extracts into tofu and soy sauce (shoyu). Other fermented foods include fish sauce, mole (made with chocolate), tea and coffee. Pickling keeps food from spoiling, while fermenting changes it.

cards.t: Milk, cheese and yogurt: microbes in dairy
q: why does milk spoil so easily
cards.x:
Milk begins sterile: water, minerals, protein, butterfat, lactose and other sugars. Microbes get in as it leaves the female mammal's body and from milking utensils, and because it is so nutrient-dense, it is highly susceptible to microbial growth.

Milk fermentation can be natural or induced, as in cheese or yogurt making. Cheese making is about 5000 years old, using cow, goat or sheep milk, and in some cultures horse or water buffalo milk. The first fermented dairy products were probably the result of accidental contamination with bacteria and fungi from human skin, nose or mouth. Cheese making involves yeast, bacteria and molds (multicellular fungi). Yogurt is milk fermented with bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus; kefir, koumiss and buttermilk are other fermented milks.

cards.t: Microbes as food, and fungi in food production and spoilage
q: can microbes be eaten as food
do fungi in food cause disease
cards.x:
Some microbes are food themselves. Macroscopic fungi and algae are the obvious ones: mushrooms, truffles and seaweed. Microbial additives are already used in animal feed; human versions are slower to be accepted, though "single cell protein" and other bacterial or fungal products are being researched in the United Kingdom and elsewhere. In the United States, the cyanobacterium Spirulina is added to foods such as smoothies and vitamin supplement gummies.

Fungi do not commonly cause disease, but they matter in food in two ways: production and spoilage. They are important in food (mushrooms), in medicine (they produce penicillin) and in industry (yeasts are fungi used to ferment many products). Fungal spoilage affects bread, cereals and acidic juices.

cards.t: Where foodborne microbes come from
q: where do foodborne pathogens come from
which foodborne germs come from poultry
which foodborne germs come from soil or water
cards.x:
Foodborne microbes reach food from five main sources.
- Feces, human and animal: Escherichia coli, the indicator organism of feces, in fecally contaminated meat or vegetables; norovirus and hepatitis A and E from feces and vomitus, including shellfish from feces-contaminated water.
- Animals, especially poultry: Salmonella (many animals, mainly poultry and aquatic reptiles), Campylobacter (raw poultry), Listeria (birds and mammals), and parasitic worms in venison, pork and other meat contaminated while the animal is still alive, or in pet feces.
- Soil and plants: Listeria persists in soil; Clostridium spores are found in soils, on plants and in honey.
- Water: Vibrio in salty ocean and estuarine waters; protozoa in drinking water and on uncooked fruits and vegetables.
- People: norovirus spreads person to person, a carrier cook can spread infection, and milk picks up microbes as it leaves the animal and from utensils.

cards.t: How big a problem foodborne illness is, and its symptoms
q: how many foodborne pathogens are there
what are the symptoms of food poisoning
cards.x:
There are an estimated 250 different foodborne pathogens, and bacteria are the most common. The figures usually given are 75 million cases a year, probably under-reported, and at least 5000 deaths, a serious problem for global health. Those figures are often labeled worldwide, but they match older United States estimates; World Health Organization estimates for the world are far larger.

The concern is not only bacteria from plant and animal sources but also viruses, parasites and toxins produced by microorganisms. The usual symptoms of foodborne illness are diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, fever and vomiting.

cards.t: Who watches food safety: health departments, CDC, FDA and USDA
q: which agencies enforce food safety law
what does the USDA do for food safety
cards.x:
Food safety in the United States has two jobs, shared among a few agencies.
- Surveillance and outbreak investigation: local and state health departments, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).
- Law enforcement and policy: the Food and Drug Administration and the United States Department of Agriculture.

So health departments and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention track and investigate, while the Food and Drug Administration and the Department of Agriculture both investigate and make and enforce the rules.

cards.t: The main foodborne bacteria (and the non-bacterial agents)
q: what are the main foodborne pathogens
what non-bacterial organisms cause foodborne illness
cards.x:
Bacteria are the most common of the estimated 250 foodborne pathogens, and seven are the better-known ones: Escherichia coli, Salmonella species, Campylobacter jejuni, Listeria monocytogenes, Clostridium species, Bacillus cereus, and Vibrio species such as vulnificus or parahaemolyticus.

Food can also carry organisms other than bacteria: fungi, protozoa, parasitic worms (in pork, venison and wild-caught fish) and viruses. On top of the organisms themselves, toxins produced by microorganisms are part of the problem.

cards.t: Food intoxication versus food infection
q: what is the difference between food intoxication and food infection
is botulism an intoxication or an infection
cards.x:
The difference is whether you swallow a ready-made toxin or live bacteria.
- Food intoxication: the bacteria make a toxin in the food, so the person eats a preformed toxin (cells and toxin together). The toxin is ingested and reaches its target organs, such as the brain and muscles. Examples: staphylococcal toxin and Clostridium botulinum toxin.
- Food infection: the person eats live bacterial cells. Improper cooking lets the bacteria multiply in the food, and after they are eaten they cause an intestinal infection. Examples: Salmonella and Listeria.

So in an intoxication the harmful toxin is already made before the food is eaten; in an infection the bacteria themselves have to set up the infection in the intestine.

cards.t: Escherichia coli in food: indicator organism and EMB plates
q: why is E. coli called an indicator organism
how is E. coli confirmed in food or water
what does E. coli look like on an EMB plate
how does E. coli get into food
cards.x:
Escherichia coli is an "indicator organism" associated with human and animal feces, so finding it in food or water points to fecal contamination. Eosin methylene blue (EMB) plates are often used to confirm it in food and water samples, where it grows with a green metallic sheen.

It is found everywhere, including inside humans, and is not always pathogenic; it has many good traits too. The bad strains, such as the enterotoxigenic or enterohemorrhagic ones, can carry numerous toxins, and as an infectious agent it causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Sporadic outbreaks originate from fecally contaminated meats or vegetables, and one of the worst culprits is one particular serotype (strain type), the one labeled with an O number and an H number.

cards.t: E. coli food outbreaks and recalls
q: what foods have caused E. coli outbreaks
what was the Jack in the Box outbreak
can lettuce cause E. coli outbreaks
cards.x:
Escherichia coli outbreaks come from fecally contaminated meats and vegetables, and the recall list shows how varied the foods are.
- Beef: the Jack in the Box hamburgers (1993), beef products (2019) and ground beef from packing companies (2023-2025).
- Leafy greens: California bagged spinach (2006) and romaine lettuce (2010, 2018 from Arizona, and 2020-2021 from California); a 2013 report found 7% of fresh spinach in grocery stores carrying Escherichia coli.
- Refrigerated cookie dough (2009).
- Raw milk cheese in the western United States (September-October 2026).

The lesson: it is not just undercooked meat. Produce, dough and dairy can carry it too.

cards.t: Salmonella as a foodborne pathogen (salmonellosis)
q: who is most at risk from Salmonella
how long is the Salmonella incubation period
cards.x:
Salmonella is a foodborne bacterium associated with many animals, mainly poultry and aquatic reptiles. The main species are Salmonella typhi, S. enterica, S. enteritidis and S. typhimurium; others are named for where they were first found, such as S. miami, S. heidelberg and S. sandiego.

Salmonellosis can appear as gastroenteritis, enteric fever, septicemia (blood infection), fever, shock and kidney dysfunction, and incubation can be as short as hours or as long as weeks. Young children and the elderly are at greatest risk. Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, is the most severe enteric fever: the bacteria invade the intestinal wall and can spread to the blood and lymph nodes.

cards.t: Salmonella food sources, recalls and Typhoid Mary
cards.x:
Salmonella sources include poultry products (chicken, turkey, duck), eggs, pet food, live poultry such as backyard hens, peanut butter and sushi-grade seafood. Recalls show it is not just an animal-food problem: peanuts and peanut butter (2009), hydrolyzed vegetable protein (2010), farm eggs (2010), ground turkey (2011), pre-cut watermelon (2018), turkey and pork products (2019), onions from Mexico (2021), pre-cut cantaloupe (2023), cucumbers from Florida and Mexico (2025) and jalapeno peppers (August 2026).

People can be the source too. "Typhoid Mary" was Mary Mallon, a cook. She was warned and given an explanation; nevertheless, she persisted, and caused multiple deadly outbreaks.

cards.t: Campylobacter jejuni
q: how many Campylobacter cells does it take to cause illness
cards.x:
Campylobacter jejuni is a leading cause of bacterial diarrheal disease each year in the United States, especially in children. It causes fever, headache, dizziness and bloody diarrhea, usually with a rapid onset, and it is very much under-reported.

It reaches people through chickens and water, cattle and milk, and poultry meat, all ending in the human gut. The infectious dose is less than 500 bacterial cells, so even one drop of raw poultry fluid can cause illness. That is why care with Thanksgiving poultry and leftovers matters.

cards.t: Listeria monocytogenes and listeriosis
q: who is at highest risk from Listeria
is Listeria the number one cause of food-related deaths
cards.x:
Listeria monocytogenes is a foodborne bacterium found in birds and mammals that can persist in soil. Pregnant women, unborn children, premature babies, elderly people and the immunocompromised are at greatest risk of listeriosis. The most vulnerable foods are soft cheeses, raw fruit and vegetables, raw or undercooked meats, deli meats, seafood and smoked seafood, hot dogs and preserved meats. It has caused large-scale recalls, including the big ice cream recall of 2016 (Blue Bell), cantaloupes, frozen vegetables and poultry (2019).

Listeria is called the number one cause of food-related deaths in the United States. Standard references differ: national estimates rank nontyphoidal Salmonella above Listeria for total deaths, though Listeria has one of the highest death rates per case.

cards.t: Why Listeria is dangerous: cold growth and spread to the fetus
q: can Listeria grow in the refrigerator
at what temperature does Listeria grow
how does Listeria reach the brain or the fetus
can Listeria grow in the freezer
cards.x:
Probably the biggest concern with Listeria is that refrigeration does not stop it. It grows well from 1 to 40 °C, so it multiplies easily at refrigerator temperature as well as at room temperature. The freezer is different: it is below the 1 °C floor of that range, and there Listeria survives rather than grows.

Once eaten, it travels: from the contaminated food to the intestine, then a lymph node, then the bloodstream (reaching the liver and spleen), and on to the brain. It can also cross the placenta to the fetus, which fits with pregnant women and unborn children being among those at greatest risk.

cards.t: Clostridium and botulism
q: how does botulinum toxin cause paralysis
why is honey linked to botulism
cards.x:
Clostridium species are Gram-positive rods that are strict anaerobes (they grow only without oxygen) and form spores. The notable food-related ones are Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium perfringens; Clostridium tetani and Clostridium difficile are not food-related. The spores are found in soils, associated with plants, and even in honey.

When the spores germinate, they can start producing botulinum toxin, the toxin also known as "botox." Botulism is known to occur in foodborne and wound-borne forms. Ingesting the toxin leads to paralysis of the muscles in the relaxed position (a limp paralysis), then respiratory failure and death. Even if only a few bacteria are present, they can produce plenty of toxin.

cards.t: Bacillus cereus: the diarrheal and emetic forms
q: which Bacillus cereus toxin is heat stable
what foods cause Bacillus cereus food poisoning
how fast does Bacillus cereus cause symptoms
cards.x:
Bacillus cereus is a very common food poisoning agent, especially in summertime. Its gastroenteritis comes in two forms:
- Diarrheal: a heat-stable toxin, linked to meat.
- Emetic (vomiting): a heat-labile toxin (one broken down by heat), linked to rice.

The intoxication has a rapid onset, 6 hours or less, with vomiting and abdominal cramps that resolve on their own. The prevention message is simple: keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold. Standard references give the reverse pairing, with the emetic (rice) toxin heat-stable and the diarrheal (meat) toxin heat-labile.

cards.t: Vibrio and seafood (cholerae, vulnificus, parahaemolyticus)
q: how do you get a Vibrio infection
what is the R-month rule for oysters
cards.x:
Vibrio are salt-tolerant bacteria of ocean and estuarine (where rivers meet the sea) waters. The species include Vibrio cholerae, V. vulnificus and V. parahaemolyticus.

They reach people by two major routes: water, either swallowed or through wound infections, and food, such as shellfish, crabs, raw seafood and oysters. The old "R-month" rule says not to eat oysters, clams or mussels in May, June, July and August, the months without an R. Whether it still holds is "maybe, maybe not": aquaculture (seafood farming) practices have advanced so much that there are fewer worries.

cards.t: Foodborne protozoa and parasitic worms
q: how do you get parasitic worms from food
how do you kill parasites in meat
cards.x:
Besides bacteria and viruses, food can carry protozoa and parasitic worms; fungi rarely cause foodborne disease and matter mostly for food production and spoilage.
- Protozoa: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia and Entamoeba. All can cause mild, usually self-limiting diarrhea, associated with uncooked fruits and vegetables or drinking water. Ready-to-eat salad bags are a common culprit.
- Parasitic worms: tapeworm, roundworm and trichinosis. Venison, pork and other meats can be contaminated while the animal is still alive, so muscle or organ meats may be suspect, and domestic pet feces can carry tapeworm and roundworm. They are best killed by thorough cooking.

cards.t: Norovirus
q: why does norovirus spread so easily
cards.x:
Norovirus is a common foodborne agent, with upwards of 23 million cases a year. It spreads person to person through feces and vomitus, which is why it moves through daycares, nursing homes and cruise ships, and also through contaminated shellfish from feces-contaminated water.

Only a few viral particles make an infectious dose. The illness comes on fast and is short: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and a low-grade fever. Prevention is good handwashing and diaper hygiene, cooking food thoroughly, and clean drinking water.

cards.t: Foodborne hepatitis (hepatitis A and E)
q: which hepatitis viruses spread through food
when is hepatitis A most contagious
how do you prevent foodborne hepatitis
cards.x:
Hepatitis viruses A through E exist, but A and E are the ones typically spread by the fecal-oral route, meaning traces of feces end up in the mouth, for example through contaminated food or water. They are not spread by kissing, sneezing, saliva or blood.

The tricky part is timing: a person is most contagious about two weeks before symptoms appear, so they can pass it on before anyone knows they are sick. Prevention is good handwashing, cooking food thoroughly and clean drinking water, and for hepatitis there is also a vaccine for use after a suspected exposure. That vaccine fits hepatitis A; there is no licensed hepatitis E vaccine in the United States.

cards.t: PulseNet and pulsed-field gel electrophoresis outbreak tracking
q: how are foodborne outbreaks traced to a source
what does pulsed-field gel electrophoresis show
cards.x:
PulseNet is a database run through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that links cases of foodborne illness. A pulsed-field gel electrophoresis pattern, a banding pattern, is made for each microbial isolate and added to the database.

When isolates share one banding pattern, that ties the cases to a common source. In one Escherichia coli investigation in Minnesota in 2010, the patient, environmental and animal isolates all shared a single pattern, while a 2005 patient's pattern differed. This surveillance helps determine the causes of outbreaks, can even detect problems at food processing plants, and reduces both the detection time and the number of cases of illness. Recall information comes from the Food and Drug Administration (food and dietary supplements, including pet food) and the United States Department of Agriculture. PulseNet has since moved from pulsed-field patterns to whole genome sequencing.

cards.t: Preventing foodborne illness: what you can do
q: how can you prevent food poisoning
what temperature should meat be cooked to
cards.x:
Preventing foodborne illness comes down to everyday habits.
- Wash hands well with hot, soapy water, and wash fruits and vegetables.
- Clean kitchen surfaces and utensils with mild bleach cleaning solutions, and avoid cross-contamination of cutting boards and utensils.
- Use a meat thermometer (165 °F) rather than guessing, and keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold.
- In food service: proper use of disposable gloves, hair coverings and food service attire, and "ServSafe" training and certification.
- When in doubt, toss it out.

Standard food-safety references differ on the thermometer: they give 165 °F for poultry, leftovers and casseroles, and lower internal temperatures for other meats.

cards.t: Parasitology and why parasites matter
q: who is most at risk from parasites
cards.x:
Parasitology is the study of eukaryotic parasites, which come in two big groups: protozoa (single-celled microbes) and helminths (worms). Eukaryotic means their cells have a nucleus and internal compartments, like ours, rather than being bacteria. Parasites cause 20% of all infectious diseases.

They are less common in industrialized countries, but they are becoming more common in people with human immunodeficiency virus infection and in other immunocompromised patients, whose immune systems are weakened.

cards.t: Neglected parasitic infections (the five priority diseases)
k: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention parasite priorities
q: which parasitic infections are called neglected
how does the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention choose parasite priorities
cards.x:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention sets public health priorities by three things: the number of people infected, the severity of the illness, and the ability to prevent and treat it. Its list of neglected parasitic infections names five diseases:
- Chagas disease, from Trypanosoma cruzi.
- Cysticercosis, from Taenia solium (the pork tapeworm).
- Toxocariasis, from Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati (the dog and cat roundworms).
- Toxoplasmosis, from Toxoplasma gondii.
- Trichomoniasis, from Trichomonas vaginalis.
Three of the five are protozoa (Chagas disease, toxoplasmosis, trichomoniasis); the other two are worm infections.

cards.t: One-line hooks for each protozoan
k: which protozoan goes with which clue
q: how do I tell the protozoa apart
what is the key clue for each protozoan
which vector goes with which protozoan
cards.x:
Each protozoan has a one-line hook worth memorizing. Gut, water and contact: Entamoeba histolytica spreads by the fecal-oral route; Naegleria fowleri is prevalent in Florida's freshwater lakes; Acanthamoeba is found in contact lens wearers; Balantidium coli comes from pigs and cattle; Giardia lamblia is common in campers; Trichomonas vaginalis is the most common curable sexually transmitted disease in young women; Cryptosporidium is tied to a major outbreak in Wisconsin from unpurified water and is named as an agent for bioterrorism.

Blood and tissue protozoa are about the carrier: tsetse fly for Trypanosoma brucei, reduviid (kissing) bug for Trypanosoma cruzi, sand fly with the dog as alternate host for Leishmania, Anopheles mosquito for Plasmodium. For Toxoplasma, think of the cat box and the fetus.

cards.t: Protozoa: the four groups and their life cycles
q: what are the groups of protozoa
what is the difference between ciliates and flagellates
cards.x:
Protozoa are single-celled, animal-like microbes, and most can move. There are an estimated 100,000 species, but only about 25 are important pathogens. The easy way to sort them is by how they move:
- Amebas move with pseudopods (extensions of the cell): Entamoeba histolytica, Naegleria fowleri, Acanthamoeba.
- Ciliates carry tufts of cilia: Balantidium coli.
- Flagellates use flagella (Trichomonas also has an undulating membrane): Trichomonas, Giardia, and the hemoflagellates Trypanosoma and Leishmania.
- Apicomplexa lack locomotor organelles as trophozoites (the active feeding cells): Plasmodium, Toxoplasma, Cryptosporidium, plus Sarcocystis, Isospora, Cyclospora and Babesia among the coccidians.

Life cycles vary. Most multiply by simple cell division of the trophozoite, many form cysts, and others have a complex cycle with asexual and sexual phases.

cards.t: Where each protozoan comes from
q: where do protozoan infections come from
which protozoa are free-living in water
cards.x:
Where a protozoan comes from tells you how you are likely to catch it:
- Human source: Entamoeba (human, with water and food), Trichomonas (human), Plasmodium (human, with a vector).
- Free-living in water: Naegleria and Acanthamoeba, which cause the brain infections.
- Zoonotic (animal source): Balantidium from pigs; Giardia through water and food.
- Vector-borne (carried by a biting insect): the hemoflagellates and malaria.
- Gut coccidians: Cryptosporidium (listed as free-living, in water and food), Isospora (dogs and other mammals), Cyclospora (water and fresh produce).

Toxoplasma is listed as zoonotic and vector-borne in that overview, but its own description names cat feces, raw meat and spread across the placenta.

cards.t: Antiprotozoan drugs: few and toxic
q: how many drugs are there for protozoa
what problems do antiprotozoan drugs have
cards.x:
Antiprotozoan drugs are relatively few compared with antibacterial drugs, and they carry toxicity problems and severe side effects. Two facts sit side by side here: these drugs work against eukaryotic cells, and the parasite's cells are eukaryotic, like ours.

One group worth remembering: Entamoeba, Giardia and Trichomonas are anaerobic protozoa that lack mitochondria (the cell's energy-making compartments).

cards.t: Entamoeba histolytica: the organism and how people catch it
q: who is at risk for amebiasis
cards.x:
Entamoeba histolytica is an ameba that lives in humans and causes amebiasis. It alternates between two forms: a large trophozoite, the active feeding form that moves with pseudopods, and a smaller nonmotile cyst. The name describes the damage it can do: histo means tissue and lytica means lysis, so the name means tissue-dissolving.

Humans are the primary host. About 10% of the world population carries it without symptoms, and it kills 100,000 people per year. People get it by the fecal-oral route: they swallow cysts, with water and food as the source. It is prevalent in tropical countries, related to fertilization practices and sewage treatment. Epidemics sometimes occur in crowded populations where water supplies are polluted, such as prisons, hospitals and juvenile care institutions, and it is sometimes sexually transmitted.

cards.t: Entamoeba histolytica life cycle (cyst to trophozoite and back)
q: what is the life cycle of Entamoeba histolytica
what happens to the cysts after you swallow them
cards.x:
The cycle is cyst in, trophozoite causes disease, cyst out. Swallowed cysts pass through the stomach and reach the small intestine. There the alkaline pH and digestive juices stimulate each cyst to release 4 trophozoites. The trophozoites attach, multiply, move about and feed, and this active phase is when disease happens.

Later the trophozoites turn back into cysts in the large intestine. The cysts are produced after the active phase of disease and leave in the feces, ready to infect the next person who swallows them.

cards.t: Amebiasis: intestinal vs extraintestinal disease
q: what are the two forms of amebiasis
what does Entamoeba histolytica do in the body
cards.x:
Amebiasis is infection with Entamoeba histolytica. In 90% of patients it causes no symptoms; severity depends on the strain, the amount of inoculum (the dose swallowed) and host conditions. When it does cause disease, it takes two forms:
- Intestinal: in the cecum, appendix, colon and rectum. The ameba may secrete enzymes that dissolve tissue and penetrate deeper layers of the lining. Signs are dysentery, abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea and weight loss. It can be life-threatening: hemorrhage, perforation, appendicitis, and tumorlike growths called amebomas.
- Extraintestinal: amebas invade organs of the peritoneal cavity, most commonly the liver, where they produce abscesses with active trophozoites (amebic hepatitis). They can also reach the lungs (pulmonary amebiasis), spleen, adrenals, kidneys, skin and brain. Severe forms have a 10% fatality rate.

cards.t: Amebiasis: diagnosis and prevention
q: why is amebiasis confused with bacillary dysentery
cards.x:
Amebiasis has symptoms similar to bacillary dysentery (the bacterial kind), so symptoms alone cannot settle it. Diagnosis rests on three things: examination of a fecal smear, an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay using monoclonal antibodies, and the patient's history.

Treatment includes medicines that work inside the intestine and others that work in the tissues, plus antidiarrheals and replacement of fluid and electrolytes. Prevention is water treatment; a vaccine is under development.

cards.t: Naegleria fowleri: where it lives and how it gets in
q: how do people get infected with Naegleria
what are the stages of Naegleria
cards.x:
Naegleria fowleri is a free-living ameba, meaning it lives in the environment instead of depending on a host. It ordinarily inhabits standing water with a high bacterial count: hot springs, lakes and streams, and unchlorinated swimming pools. Over 46% of lakes in Florida have it. It shows up in three stages: a round, walled cyst, a trophozoite with pseudopods, and a flagellated stage. The trophozoite is the stage that invades people.

It gets in through the nose. Most cases are children and young adults after exposure to freshwater lakes and streams: diving, waterskiing, jetskiing. It has also followed rinsing the sinuses, even with tap water.

cards.t: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis (Naegleria brain infection)
q: what are the symptoms of a Naegleria infection
how do you prevent Naegleria infection
cards.x:
Primary amebic meningoencephalitis is the brain infection caused by Naegleria fowleri. The trophozoite burrows through the lining of the nose and travels into the brain along the olfactory nerve. It starts with headache, respiratory symptoms, fever, vomiting and stiff neck. Then comes rapid destruction of the brain and spinal cord: confusion, lack of balance, hallucinations, coma, and death in 3-7 days.

It is rare but almost always fatal; the historical fatality rate is more than 97%, and treatment must be early. Prevention: do not swim or dive in unchlorinated water, and use nose plugs.

cards.t: Naegleria cases: who, where and when
q: where in the United States are Naegleria cases
cards.x:
Naegleria infection is rare, nearly always fatal, seen in summer, and mostly in the South. The typical annual case count in the United States is fewer than 10, and 73% of cases occur in July and August. Texas and Florida have the most confirmed cases, and the age and sex group with the most cases is males aged 10-14. Most cases occur in the southern United States, but rising temperatures have created favorable environments farther north.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that more people are infected than reported, with perhaps 70-80% going undiagnosed. The historical fatality rate is more than 97%, and only 4 survivors are known in the United States.

cards.t: Entamoeba vs Naegleria vs Acanthamoeba
q: what is the difference between Naegleria and Acanthamoeba
how do the three amebas differ
which ameba enters through the nose
cards.x:
The three amebas differ in where they live, how they get in, and what they attack:
- Entamoeba histolytica: human source, caught by swallowing cysts (fecal-oral route); attacks the intestine and can spread to the liver and other organs.
- Naegleria fowleri: free-living in standing water such as lakes, hot springs and unchlorinated pools; enters through the nose and climbs the olfactory nerve into the brain; death in 3-7 days, fatality more than 97%.
- Acanthamoeba: free-living in water and soil; enters through the eye (keratitis in contact lens wearers) or through broken skin or the nose (granulomatous amebic encephalitis).

Quick way to separate the two free-living ones: Naegleria is fast and comes through the nose; Acanthamoeba has more ways in and a slower course, with survival of only 2-3% for the brain infection.

cards.t: Acanthamoeba: keratitis and granulomatous amebic encephalitis
q: how does Acanthamoeba infect the eye
how does granulomatous amebic encephalitis differ from Naegleria
cards.x:
Acanthamoeba is a free-living ameba found worldwide in freshwater lakes, hot tubs, swimming pools, soil and water. It causes two separate diseases:
- Amebic keratitis: an eye infection in contact lens wearers, with eye pain, redness and irritation. It does not typically spread beyond the eye.
- Granulomatous amebic encephalitis: a brain infection. The ameba typically enters through a break in the skin or through the nasal passages. Symptoms look like meningitis but progress over a longer time, and survival is only 2-3%. In people with compromised immune systems it can also disseminate (spread through the body) or cause skin lesions.

The drugs tried against it are only tentatively successful.

cards.t: Balantidium coli and balantidiosis
cards.x:
Balantidium coli is the one ciliate among these protozoa: its trophozoite carries tufts of cilia, tiny hair-like projections. It lives in the intestines of domestic animals such as pigs and cattle. People get it by ingesting cyst-containing food or water.

The trophozoite erodes the intestine and causes balantidiosis: persistent diarrhea, occasionally dysentery, abdominal pain and weight loss. Healthy humans are resistant, and the organism rarely penetrates the intestine or enters the blood.

cards.t: Trichomonas vaginalis: the organism
cards.x:
Trichomonas vaginalis is a small, pear-shaped flagellate with 4 flagella at the front and an undulating membrane along its side. It exists only as a trophozoite: there is no cyst stage. Its reservoir is the human urogenital tract.

It is a strict parasite that cannot survive long outside the host, and it is sexually transmitted. Three Trichomonas species infect humans: Trichomonas vaginalis, Trichomonas tenax and Trichomonas hominis.

cards.t: Trichomoniasis: disease, risks and diagnosis
q: what are the symptoms of trichomoniasis
why does trichomoniasis matter beyond the infection
cards.x:
Trichomoniasis is the most common curable sexually transmitted disease in young, sexually active women: 7.4-8 million cases a year in North America and 124 million worldwide. Between 60% and 70% of infected people have no symptoms. The incubation period is 4-28 days.
- Women: foul-smelling, green-to-yellow discharge; vulvitis; cervicitis; urinary frequency and pain.
- Men: urethritis; a thin, milky discharge; occasionally prostate infection.

It matters beyond the infection itself. It may predispose to other sexually transmitted diseases, raises cervical cancer risk 2-3 times, and increases human immunodeficiency virus transmission by 50%. Diagnosis is by microscopic analysis of a vaginal smear, and 4.3% of Trichomonas are resistant to the antimicrobials.

cards.t: Giardia vs Trichomonas vs Balantidium
q: what is the difference between Giardia, Trichomonas and Balantidium
cards.x:
These three are easy to mix up, but each has a clear identity:
- Giardia lamblia: a flagellate, heart-shaped with a concave underside that works like a suction cup. It is swallowed as cysts in water and food, and causes diarrhea and abdominal pain.
- Trichomonas vaginalis: a flagellate, pear-shaped with 4 front flagella and an undulating membrane. It has no cyst, is a strict parasite that cannot survive long outside the host, and is sexually transmitted.
- Balantidium coli: the ciliate, with cilia instead of flagella. It comes from pigs and cattle through contaminated food or water and causes persistent diarrhea.

Quick way to tell: Giardia and Balantidium are swallowed as cysts; Trichomonas has no cyst and spreads by sex.

cards.t: Giardia lamblia and giardiasis
q: what are the reservoirs of Giardia
cards.x:
Giardia lamblia is a flagellate with a symmetrical heart shape and a concave underside that acts like a suction cup. The trophozoite has two nuclei. The cysts are small, compact and have several nuclei.

Reservoirs include beavers, cattle, coyotes, cats and humans, and cysts can survive for 2 months in the environment. People usually ingest them with water and food; the infectious dose is only 10 to 100 cysts, and giardiasis is common in campers. The cysts enter the duodenum, germinate, and travel to the jejunum to feed and multiply. Giardiasis causes diarrhea and abdominal pain.

cards.t: Giardia: diagnosis and prevention
q: why is giardiasis hard to diagnose under the microscope
cards.x:
Giardiasis is hard to diagnose by microscope because the organism is shed in feces intermittently. A stool sample can look clean on a day when the parasite is not being shed. Polymerase chain reaction analysis (a DNA-based test) is also used.

For prevention, the agent is killed by boiling, ozone and iodine. For context, the cysts can survive for 2 months in the environment, and the infectious dose is only 10 to 100 cysts.

cards.t: Hemoflagellates and their insect vectors
cards.x:
Hemoflagellates are flagellated parasites that live in the blood and tissues of the human host and are carried by biting insects. They are obligate parasites (they must live in a host) and cause life-threatening and debilitating zoonoses, which are diseases passed from animals to people. In specific tropical regions they are spread by blood-sucking insects that serve as intermediate hosts. Their life cycles are complicated and the parasite changes form along the way.

Match the insect to the parasite: Leishmania, sand fly; Trypanosoma brucei, tsetse fly; Trypanosoma cruzi, reduviid (kissing) bug. The route into people differs: Leishmania is found in the sand fly gut; Trypanosoma brucei is in the tsetse fly's biting mouthparts; Trypanosoma cruzi is in the feces of the reduviid bug.

cards.t: Trypanosoma brucei and African sleeping sickness
q: how does Trypanosoma brucei cause disease
how does Trypanosoma brucei avoid the immune system
what are the symptoms of sleeping sickness
cards.x:
African sleeping sickness is caused by Trypanosoma brucei and spread by tsetse flies; reservoir mammals harbor the parasite. Trypanosomes are elongate, spindle-shaped cells with tapered ends and eel-like motility.

The biting fly inoculates the skin, and a primary chancre (a sore) develops. The parasite migrates into the lymphatics, spreads in the blood, and multiplies there, damaging the spleen, lymph nodes and brain. It evades the immune response by antigenic variation, displaying over 100 different antigens. Early symptoms are fever, enlarged spleen, swollen lymph nodes and joint pain. As it moves into the central nervous system come personality and behavioral changes, then sleep disturbances, tremors, seizures, paralysis and coma.

cards.t: Gambian vs Rhodesian sleeping sickness
q: what is the difference between Gambian and Rhodesian sleeping sickness
where is Rhodesian sleeping sickness found
cards.x:
African sleeping sickness comes in two variants caused by two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei, both spread by tsetse flies:
- Gambian strain: West Africa; chronic, with brain symptoms years later.
- Rhodesian strain: East Africa; acute, with brain symptoms within 3-4 weeks.

Quick way to remember: Gambian is West and slow; Rhodesian is East and fast.

cards.t: Sleeping sickness: diagnosis and control
q: how is African sleeping sickness diagnosed
what is the card agglutination test
cards.x:
Trypanosomes are readily demonstrated in blood, spinal fluid or lymph nodes. The card agglutination test for trypanosomes gives a rapid diagnosis.

The drugs for sleeping sickness are meant to be given before neurological involvement, that is, before the parasite reaches the nervous system. Control involves eliminating the tsetse fly, the vector.

cards.t: Chagas disease: the kissing bug and how it spreads
q: how do you get Chagas disease
what is the vector for Chagas disease
is Chagas disease in the United States
cards.x:
Chagas disease, or American trypanosomiasis, is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi. There are millions of cases in Latin America, and it is becoming more of an issue in the Southern United States because the vector is migrating. The National Institutes of Health estimates 300,000 infected in the United States, and it is now considered by many to be endemic there.

The vector is the reduviid bug, the kissing bug. Infection occurs when the bug's feces are inoculated into a cutaneous portal (a break in the skin). It can also spread congenitally, through transfusions, organ transplants, or by ingesting food contaminated by triatomine urine or feces; spread by contaminated food typically results in more severe cases and higher mortality.

cards.t: Chagas disease: signs and organs affected
q: what does Trypanosoma cruzi do to the body
which organs does Chagas disease affect
how is Chagas disease treated and controlled
cards.x:
The first sign is a local lesion at the entry point: Romaña's sign, also called a chagoma, a swelling of the eyelid with conjunctivitis. Fever and swelling of the lymph nodes, spleen and liver can follow.

The parasite lives inside human cells, with masses of it in the heart muscle and the large intestine. Chronic inflammation develops in the organs, especially the heart and brain, and Chagas disease accounts for 30-40% of heart disease in endemic regions.

Treatment must be administered early. Control is through control of the vector, and a vaccine is under development.

cards.t: Trypanosoma brucei vs Trypanosoma cruzi
q: what is the difference between sleeping sickness and Chagas disease
which trypanosome is spread by the tsetse fly
how does each trypanosome enter the body
cards.x:
The two trypanosomes cause different diseases, live in different places and use different vectors:
- Trypanosoma brucei: African sleeping sickness; Africa (Gambian West, Rhodesian East); tsetse fly. The bite inoculates the parasite, a primary chancre forms, and it goes on to blood, lymph nodes, spleen and brain.
- Trypanosoma cruzi: Chagas disease; Central and South America, spreading into the Southern United States; reduviid (kissing) bug. The bug's feces are inoculated into a skin portal, and it can also pass by transfusion, transplant, mother to baby, or contaminated food. It targets the heart muscle and large intestine.

Signs to know: primary chancre and antigenic variation for sleeping sickness; Romaña's sign for Chagas disease. Control: eliminate the tsetse fly versus control the vector.

cards.t: Leishmania and leishmaniasis: how it spreads
q: why is leishmaniasis sometimes local and sometimes systemic
cards.x:
Leishmaniasis is a zoonosis (an animal disease that reaches people) passed among mammals by female sand flies, which need a blood meal to produce eggs. Dogs are the alternate hosts. It is endemic to equatorial regions: 98 countries are affected, with a global prevalence of 12 million cases and 2-2.5 million new cases a year.

The sand fly bite injects the parasite, which multiplies inside macrophages (immune cells that normally swallow invaders). If the infected macrophage does not migrate, the infection stays localized; if it migrates, the infection becomes systemic, meaning it spreads through the body. Leishmaniasis and malaria co-infection is an increasing issue and may make diagnosis difficult.

cards.t: The three forms of leishmaniasis
q: what are the forms of leishmaniasis
cards.x:
Leishmaniasis shows up in three forms:
- Cutaneous: a localized ulcerated sore, known as oriental sore or Baghdad boil.
- Espundia: infection of the skin and mucous membranes of the head. It is a chronic infection that occurs after cutaneous disease.
- Systemic (visceral): high intermittent fever, weight loss, and enlarged spleen, liver and lymph nodes. Kala azar is named as the most severe form, and it is fatal if untreated.

Kala azar is also listed by name next to Baghdad boil and espundia in the disease's list of names, so you may see it written as its own entry.

Quick way to sort them: skin sore only is cutaneous, head and mucous membranes later is espundia, whole-body illness with a big spleen and liver is the systemic form.

cards.t: Malaria: the disease and Plasmodium
cards.x:
Malaria is the dominant protozoan disease: it threatens 40% of the world's population each year. The cause is Plasmodium, an obligate intracellular sporozoan, meaning it must live inside host cells. Species named include Plasmodium malariae, vivax, falciparum and ovale; some lists give only the first three, so the number of species depends on which list you read.

The female Anopheles mosquito is the primary vector. Malaria also spreads by blood transfusions and from mother to fetus. There are 300-500 million new cases each year, 90% of them in Africa, with 2 million deaths each year and 1,000-2,000 cases a year in the United States.

cards.t: Plasmodium life cycle: liver, red blood cells, mosquito
q: what is the life cycle of Plasmodium
where does Plasmodium multiply in humans
where does sexual reproduction of malaria occur
cards.x:
Plasmodium has two distinct phases in two hosts. In the human, the cycle is asexual:
- Liver phase: the infected female mosquito injects sporozoites, which localize in the liver and undergo schizogony, a division that produces numerous merozoites, which enter the circulation in 5-16 days depending on the species.
- Red blood cell phase: merozoites enter red blood cells, become circular ring trophozoites and multiply. The red cell bursts, releasing more merozoites.
- Gamete phase: merozoites differentiate into gametes (sex cells), which are now in the blood.

The sexual phase happens in the female Anopheles mosquito. It draws infected red blood cells, the gametes fertilize, and the cell forms sporozoites in the stomach. They lodge in the salivary glands, available to infect the next human.

cards.t: Malaria: symptoms, complications and diagnosis
q: what are the symptoms of malaria
why does malaria cause fever in cycles
which malaria species is most dangerous
cards.x:
After a 10-16 day incubation period, malaria starts with malaise, fatigue, aches and nausea, and then regular episodes of chills, fever and sweating. The episodes come at 48-72 hour intervals as the red blood cells rupture and release parasites; the interval depends on the species.

Complications are anemia and enlargement of the spleen, liver and kidneys. Plasmodium falciparum is the most malignant type, with the highest death rate in children.

Diagnosis is by finding trophozoites inside red blood cells (the small ring forms on a blood smear), together with symptoms.

cards.t: Malaria: resistance, control and the vaccine
q: who is naturally resistant to malaria
what are the problems with the malaria vaccine
cards.x:
Some populations are naturally resistant to malaria: people with sickle cell trait. Drug resistance is increasing, and mosquito control is key.

A vaccine has just been approved by the World Health Organization for children. It has real challenges: a complex regimen (3 doses before the rainy season, then booster doses before later rainy seasons), getting the vaccine to the areas where it is needed, cost of the vaccine and its distribution at $325 million a year, and only about 30% effectiveness.

cards.t: Apicomplexa (sporozoans)
q: what do Plasmodium, Toxoplasma and Cryptosporidium have in common
cards.x: Apicomplexa are sporozoans: protozoa that lack locomotor organelles (structures for moving) in the trophozoite state. They alternate between sexual and asexual phases and between different animal hosts. Most form specialized infective bodies that are transmitted by arthropod vectors (insects and relatives), food, water or other means. Plasmodium, Toxoplasma and Cryptosporidium are the examples to know.

cards.t: The coccidians: what they are and who is in the group
k: Toxoplasma Sarcocystis Cryptosporidium Isospora Cyclospora Babesia
cards.x: Coccidians are apicomplexan parasites that are zoonotic in domestic animals and birds, and they exist in stages that include dormant oocysts and pseudocysts. The ones to know are Toxoplasma, Sarcocystis, Cryptosporidium, Isospora, Cyclospora and Babesia. A fast hook for each: Toxoplasma goes with cats, Sarcocystis with undercooked meat, Cryptosporidium with water, Isospora with fecally contaminated food or drink, Cyclospora with fresh produce, and Babesia with ticks.

cards.t: Toxoplasma gondii: the organism and how people get it
q: why do cats matter for toxoplasmosis
how many people have been exposed to Toxoplasma
cards.x:
Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular apicomplexan parasite with an extensive distribution, able to infect virtually all warm-blooded animals. Seroprevalence (the share with antibodies in the blood) indicates that approximately one third of the human population worldwide has been exposed.

It lives naturally in cats, the definitive host, which harbor oocysts in the gastrointestinal tract and release them through feces. People acquire it by ingesting raw meats or substances contaminated by cat feces.

cards.t: Toxoplasmosis: disease in healthy and immunocompromised people
q: what are the symptoms of toxoplasmosis
cards.x:
Most toxoplasmosis cases go unnoticed or cause mild symptoms: sore throat, fever and enlarged lymph nodes. The serious problems come in two groups.
- Immunocompromised individuals, including patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, can suffer brain and heart damage; toxoplasma encephalitis is the brain form, with a danger of central nervous system involvement.
- Congenital disease (infection of the baby before birth): spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, or severe neurological and eye problems in the newborn, including hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis.

cards.t: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy (why not to clean the cat box)
q: why should pregnant women not clean the cat box
what is the chance Toxoplasma passes to the fetus
how does Toxoplasma reach the fetus
cards.x:
When a pregnant woman has toxoplasmosis, the parasite can cross the placenta to the fetus, which is called transplacental transmission; the chance of transmission is 33%. That is the reason pregnant women should not clean the cat box: cat feces can carry the parasite's oocysts, and the danger is to the baby.

For the fetus the consequences can be spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, or a spectrum of severe neurological and eye problems in the newborn, including hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis.

cards.t: Toxoplasmosis: diagnosis, treatment and vaccine hurdles
q: why is there no toxoplasmosis vaccine
cards.x:
Toxoplasmosis is diagnosed by serological tests (blood tests for antibodies), culture and histological analysis (looking at tissue). Treatment uses two drugs together given long-term, and together they inhibit enzymes in the pathway for folate synthesis.

Vaccine development is in progress but is hampered by three things: the genetic diversity of Toxoplasma gondii strains, a life cycle with many different stages, and the need to produce a robust and balanced T helper 1 cellular immune response. A promising candidate is a genetically engineered live attenuated (weakened) strain with a crucial transcription factor blocked.

cards.t: Toxoplasma and mental health links
q: what did the hyena study show
cards.x:
Toxoplasma has been linked to mental disorders in studies. Studies link cat ownership in childhood with later development of mental illness. Acute toxoplasmosis can cause delusions and hallucinations; latent toxoplasmosis is a risk factor for schizophrenia, anxiety, and possibly obsessive compulsive disorder and addiction; chronic toxoplasmosis is linked to schizophrenia, mood disorders, psychosis and self-directed violence. One Dutch study showed twice the risk of developing schizophrenia if infected.

Animals may be affected too: in hyena and lion observation studies, Toxoplasma-infected hyena cubs are bolder, more likely to approach lions, and have a higher mortality rate. The hypothesis is that boldness in young hyenas furthers the spread of Toxoplasma into its feline definitive host.

cards.t: Sarcocystis and sarcocystosis
q: what are the symptoms of sarcocystosis
cards.x:
Sarcocystis species are parasites of cattle, swine and sheep. Two species infect humans: Sarcocystis hominis, from cattle, and Sarcocystis suihominis, from pigs. Humans can be dead-end hosts for other species.

Domestic animals are the intermediate hosts: they pick up infective cysts while grazing on grass contaminated with human feces. Humans are infected when the undercooked meat is eaten. Sarcocystis hominis and Sarcocystis suihominis cause diarrhea, nausea and abdominal pain; other species cause muscle cysts, myalgia (muscle pain), weakness and edema.

cards.t: Cryptosporidium: the organism and how it spreads
q: can Cryptosporidium survive chlorine in swimming pools
cards.x:
Cryptosporidium is an intestinal pathogen that infects a variety of mammals, birds and reptiles, and it exists in tissue and oocyst phases. An infected person or animal can shed 10-100 million parasites in a single bowel movement, and the infectious dose is as little as 10 organisms.

People most often get it by consuming water in recreational settings, or contaminated water, ice or foodstuffs. It is the leading cause of recreational waterborne disease, and the organism can tolerate chlorine in swimming pools. In the 1990s, 370,000 cases occurred in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, from contaminated water; filtration is required for removal.

cards.t: Cryptosporidiosis: what it does and who is at risk
cards.x:
After oocysts are swallowed, they release sporozoites that penetrate intestinal cells. Cryptosporidium causes gastroenteritis with headache, sweating, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhea.

Patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome and other immunocompromised people may have chronic persistent diarrhea, and young children and the elderly are likely to be infected. There are few effective drugs, and it is considered a potential agent for bioterrorism. It is also a large hidden burden: an estimated 748,000 cases a year among United States diarrheal parasites, with fewer than 2% verified in surveillance data.

cards.t: Isospora belli and coccidiosis
q: what are the symptoms of Isospora infection
cards.x:
Isospora belli is an intracellular intestinal parasite with an oocyst stage. It is transmitted in fecally contaminated food or drink, and dogs and other mammals are listed as its sources.

Infection is usually asymptomatic or self-limited. When symptoms occur they include malaise, nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, fatty stools, abdominal cramping and weight loss. The disease is primarily associated with immunocompromised hosts. Treatment is given only when required.

cards.t: Cyclospora cayetanensis and cyclosporiasis
cards.x:
Cyclospora cayetanensis is an emerging protozoan pathogen that causes cyclosporiasis. It spreads by the oral-fecal route through fresh produce and water. Oocysts enter the small intestine and invade the lining. Symptoms are watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, bloating, fever and muscle aches.

Diagnosis can be complicated: multiple stool samples must be tested, and the oocysts show up pink-red with an acid-fast stain of a fecal smear. In 2026 a widespread outbreak was linked to iceberg lettuce: from 1 May to 31 August, 20,996 laboratory-confirmed cases, 1,161 hospitalizations, 2 deaths and 49 states reporting. There were likely many more cases that were not tested or reported.

cards.t: Babesia and babesiosis
q: who is at risk for severe babesiosis
what are the symptoms of babesiosis
cards.x:
Babesia has two firsts: it was the first protozoan found to cause a disease (redwater fever of cattle, also called bovine babesiosis, Texas fever or tick fever), and the first found to be associated with a vector, the tick.

Human babesiosis is caused by Babesia microti, carried by the blacklegged deer tick, and is a relatively rare zoonosis. It starts with flu-like symptoms, but the parasite attacks red blood cells, and hemolytic anemia can result. It is serious for people without a spleen, the immunocompromised, those with pre-existing liver or kidney disease, and those older than 50.

cards.t: Coccidians compared: where each comes from and how you get it
q: how do you catch each coccidian
which coccidians come from undercooked meat
which coccidian comes from fresh produce
cards.x:
The coccidians are mostly sorted by how they reach you:
- Toxoplasma gondii: cats (the definitive host) and virtually all warm-blooded animals; raw meat or things contaminated by cat feces, and across the placenta.
- Sarcocystis: cattle, swine and sheep as intermediate hosts; undercooked meat.
- Cryptosporidium: mammals, birds and reptiles; recreational and contaminated water, ice and food; chlorine-tolerant; infectious dose as low as 10.
- Isospora belli: dogs and other mammals; fecally contaminated food or drink.
- Cyclospora cayetanensis: oral-fecal, fresh produce and water.
Babesia microti stands apart: it is carried by the blacklegged deer tick.

cards.t: Coccidians compared: what each one causes and how it is found
q: which coccidians cause chronic diarrhea in immunocompromised patients
cards.x:
What each coccidian does:
- Toxoplasmosis: mostly unnoticed; encephalitis in the immunocompromised; congenital hydrocephalus, calcifications and chorioretinitis. Found by serological tests, culture or histological analysis.
- Sarcocystosis: diarrhea, nausea and abdominal pain, or muscle cysts, myalgia, weakness and edema with other species.
- Cryptosporidiosis: gastroenteritis, with chronic persistent diarrhea in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. Few effective drugs.
- Coccidiosis (Isospora): usually asymptomatic or self-limited; diarrhea and fatty stools; mainly immunocompromised hosts.
- Cyclosporiasis: watery diarrhea, cramps, bloating, fever. Needs multiple stool samples and an acid-fast stain.
- Babesiosis: flu-like illness and hemolytic anemia; serious without a spleen.

cards.t: Helminths: what they are and where infection comes from
q: how do people get worm infections
how do helminth life cycles work
cards.x:
Helminths are parasitic worms. Unlike one-celled protozoa, adult worms are large, many-celled animals with specialized tissues and organs. Adults mate and produce fertilized eggs; the eggs hatch, and the larvae (the immature forms) mature through several stages into adults. In some species the sexes are separate, and in others the worm is hermaphroditic, meaning one worm has both sets of reproductive organs.

People are infected through contaminated food, soil or water, or through infected animals. However different the worms look, their life cycles fall into just four basic patterns, called cycles A to D, of how the worm moves through its hosts and into people.

cards.t: Definitive, intermediate and transport hosts
q: what is the difference between a definitive and an intermediate host
cards.x:
The three host types are told apart by what the worm does inside them.

- Definitive host: the worm reaches adulthood and mates here.
- Intermediate host: larval development takes place here.
- Transport host: the worm experiences no parasitic development at all. It is simply carried along on the way to the definitive host. This is the same thing as a paratenic host, a host in which the organism does not grow.

Quick way to sort any host: ask what the worm is doing in it. Growing up and mating means definitive; developing as a larva means intermediate; doing nothing but being carried means transport.

cards.t: Life cycles A and B: eggs swallowed vs larvae through the skin
q: what is life cycle A for worms
how is cycle B different from cycle A
which worms enter through the skin
cards.x:
Cycles A and B differ in how the worm gets in.

In the "eggs swallowed" pattern (cycle A), a person swallows mature eggs in contaminated food or water. The larvae hatch, burrow through tissue, may travel to the lungs and then the pharynx (throat), and are swallowed. The adults finish the cycle in the intestine, and eggs leave in the feces. Ascaris lumbricoides and Trichuris trichiura follow this pattern.

In the "larvae through the skin" pattern (cycle B), infective larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through tissue to the lungs and throat, and are swallowed. They reproduce in the intestine, eggs go out in feces into the soil, and infective larvae in the soil complete the cycle. The hookworms and Strongyloides stercoralis follow this pattern. Simple split: a swallowed egg versus a larva that comes through your skin.

cards.t: Life cycles C and D: encysted worm in meat vs intermediate host
q: what is life cycle C for worms
what is life cycle D for worms
which worms use an intermediate host
cards.x:
The other two patterns involve an animal.

In the "encysted worm in meat" pattern (cycle C), a person eats the encysted worm in muscle, which means undercooked meat. Passage through the stomach frees the larva from its cyst, and the worms mature and make eggs that leave in the feces. A food animal grazes on grass contaminated with feces, the worm encysts in its muscle, and the cysts are in the meat when the animal is slaughtered. Trichinella spiralis and the tapeworms are placed in this pattern, although the letter given to a particular worm can differ between descriptions.

In the "intermediate host" pattern (cycle D), a middle host is involved. The first larval stage infects the intermediate host, which releases a second-stage, infective larva into water, or, if the intermediate host is a biting insect, passes it on through its bite. Examples: Wuchereria bancrofti, Onchocerca volvulus, Loa loa, Schistosoma, and the liver and lung flukes Opisthorchis and Paragonimus.

cards.t: Egg-infective vs larva-infective intestinal roundworms
k: which roundworms are infective as eggs
q: which intestinal worms are infective as eggs
which intestinal roundworms are infective as larvae
what is the difference between egg-infective and larva-infective worms
cards.x:
Intestinal roundworms are grouped by which stage is infective.

- Infective in the egg stage: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), Ascaris lumbricoides and Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm). You swallow the egg. Whipworm and Ascaris spread by fecal pollution of soil with eggs; pinworm spreads by close contact and contaminated objects (fomites).
- Infective in the larval stage: the hookworms Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, the threadworm Strongyloides stercoralis, and Trichinella spiralis.

The easy mistake is to assume everything that comes from contaminated soil is swallowed as an egg. For the hookworms and Strongyloides, the infective larvae go in through the skin, and Trichinella is taken in as larvae in meat.

cards.t: How worms damage the body, and the main defense
q: what is the immune defense against worms
cards.x:
Worms are well equipped to live in a host. They have specialized mouthparts for attachment, enzymes that break down (hydrolyze) tissue, and a cuticle (tough outer covering) that protects against immune defenses, and their organ systems are reduced.

The damage comes from three things: worms feeding on and migrating through tissues, worms accumulating in organs and causing blockages, and toxic worm secretions. The results include enlargement and swelling of organs, hemorrhage (bleeding), weight loss and anemia.

The defense against worms is the eosinophil, a white blood cell. Even so, worms are often difficult to eliminate completely without drugs.

cards.t: Diagnosing worm infections and how anti-worm drugs work
q: do antihelminthic drugs have side effects
cards.x:
Several clues point to a worm infection. A blood cell count can show eosinophilia, a raised number of eosinophils. Serological (blood-based) tests can be used. The direct proof is finding eggs, larvae or adult worms in feces, sputum, urine, blood or tissue biopsies.

Antihelminthic drugs (anti-worm drugs) work in a few ways. They suppress a worm metabolic process that differs from the human process, they inhibit the worm's movement, or they stop it from holding its position. They act locally in the intestine. Many antihelminthic drugs have toxic side effects.

cards.t: Nematodes (roundworms): what they are and the two groups
q: what are the groups of roundworms
what is the body plan of a roundworm
cards.x:
Nematodes are roundworms, one of the most abundant animal groups, with 50 species that affect humans. The body is elongated and cylindrical, with a protective cuticle, circular muscles and a complete digestive tract (a gut running from mouth to anus), and the sexes are separate.

Medically they split into two groups by where they live. Intestinal nematodes include Ascaris, whipworm, pinworm, the hookworms and the threadworm. Tissue nematodes complete their life cycle in human blood, lymphatics or skin; these are the filarial worms Wuchereria bancrofti, Onchocerca volvulus and Loa loa.

cards.t: Ascaris lumbricoides (large intestinal roundworm)
q: what is the life cycle of Ascaris
cards.x:
Ascaris lumbricoides is a large intestinal roundworm that causes ascariasis. It is indigenous to humans and spends its larval and adult stages in them. Most cases in the United States are in the southeastern states.

People get it by swallowing eggs. Eggs leave in feces and spread to other people through food, drink or contaminated objects. Swallowed eggs hatch into larvae, which burrow through the intestine into the circulation, travel to the lungs and pharynx, and are swallowed. Adult worms complete the cycle in the intestine and reproduce at about 200,000 eggs a day. Diagnosis is by microscopic or macroscopic analysis, meaning the eggs or the worms are looked for directly.

cards.t: Ascaris disease: lung migration, obstruction and growth effects
q: why does Ascaris cause lung symptoms
cards.x:
Ascaris worms do not attach to the gut. They keep moving, and severe inflammatory reactions mark the route they migrate along. Allergic reactions can also occur.

When the larvae travel through the lungs, they may cause pulmonary symptoms, specifically eosinophilic pneumonitis, lung inflammation with many eosinophils.

Heavy worm loads can cause abdominal pain and intestinal obstruction, as a mass of worms can pack the intestine. The infection may also retard physical and mental development. Three things to attach to Ascaris: lung migration with eosinophilic pneumonitis, obstruction with heavy loads, and effects on development.

cards.t: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm)
cards.x:
Trichuris trichiura is the whipworm, and the disease is trichuriasis. Humans are the sole host. It is most common in the tropics, and in the United States it is found in the South.

People swallow eggs from fecal pollution of soil. The eggs hatch in the intestines, and the larvae attach, penetrate the outer wall and develop into adults. Females lay 3,000 to 5,000 eggs daily.

The worms can pierce capillaries and cause localized hemorrhage (bleeding). Heavy infestations can cause dysentery and rectal prolapse, where the rectum slips out of place, and can be fatal in children. The egg is oval and barrel-shaped with a knob at each end.

cards.t: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) and the tape test
q: why does pinworm cause anal itching
cards.x:
Enterobius vermicularis is the pinworm, or seatworm, and the disease is enterobiasis. It is the most common worm disease of children in temperate zones and is very common in daycare settings.

People pick up eggs from their surroundings and swallow them, through close contact and contaminated objects (fomites). Self-inoculation, where a person re-infects themselves, is common. The eggs hatch in the small intestine and develop into adults. At night the mature female migrates out to the perianal region to lay eggs, and anal itching occurs when she emerges to release them.

Diagnosis uses the tape test (the Scotch tape test): clear tape picks up eggs from the perianal folds.

cards.t: Hookworms: Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale
q: how do hookworm larvae reach the intestine
cards.x:
Hookworms are small intestinal roundworms with curved ends and hooked mouths. Two species infect people: Necator americanus (the New World hookworm) and Ancylostoma duodenale (the Old World hookworm).

The route in is the skin, not the mouth. Humans shed eggs in feces, and the larvae that develop in the soil burrow into the skin, typically of bare feet (the soles). They travel in the blood to the lungs, go up the bronchi and throat, and are swallowed. The worms mature and reproduce in the small intestine and complete the cycle. Eggs in feces are the diagnostic stage.

cards.t: Hookworm disease: blood loss and anemia
cards.x:
Hookworm infection can cause pneumonia, nausea, vomiting, cramps and bloody diarrhea. The feature to remember is blood loss: it is significant, and anemia results.

The larvae enter through the skin of bare feet, and eggs in the feces are the diagnostic stage.

cards.t: Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) and eosinophilic meningitis
q: how do people get Angiostrongylus cantonensis
how is eosinophilic meningitis different from bacterial meningitis
cards.x:
Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm, is a nematode that causes eosinophilic meningitis. Snails are intermediate hosts. People get it by ingesting contaminated snails, water or vegetables, in other words by eating the larvae.

The incubation period is 1 day to 6 weeks, and the symptoms look like bacterial meningitis: nausea, vomiting, headaches and stiff neck. A lumbar puncture shows elevated eosinophils instead of neutrophils.

Some patients recover on their own because the parasite does not survive long in the human body; others experience coma and death. Prevention is snail and slug control and washing contaminated fruits and vegetables.

cards.t: Strongyloides stercoralis (threadworm)
k: worm that reinfects the same host
cards.x:
Strongyloides stercoralis is the threadworm, a tiny roundworm that can complete its life cycle in humans or in moist soil. Larvae penetrate the skin, migrate to the lungs, are swallowed and finish development in the intestine, the same route in as for hookworm.

What sets it apart is that it can reinfect the same host without leaving the body: larvae can start another round inside the same person.

Heavy worm loads can cause pneumonitis and eosinophilia, bloody diarrhea, liver enlargement, bowel obstruction and malabsorption (poor uptake of nutrients from the gut).

cards.t: Trichinella spiralis (trichinellosis)
q: where does Trichinella go in the body
cards.x:
Trichinella spiralis causes trichinellosis, also called trichinosis. People get it by eating undercooked pork or bear meat that contains larvae. Pigs and wild mammals are its hosts.

Larvae encysted in animal muscle are the infective stage. When a person eats them, the cysts hatch and the worms mature in the intestinal lining. The adults reproduce and make new larvae, which burrow through the intestine and enter the circulation. The larvae then migrate from the intestine to blood vessels, muscle, heart and brain, where they form cysts. In skeletal muscle the cysts can remain for years.

Symptoms come from the larvae encysting in muscle, and there is no cure after the larvae have encysted.

cards.t: Trichinellosis symptoms: two phases and dangerous complications
q: what are the symptoms of trichinosis
what are the two phases of trichinellosis
where do Trichinella larvae go and what do they cause
cards.x:
Trichinellosis shows up in two waves. The first symptoms are flulike, with diarrhea. The second symptoms are muscle and joint pain, shortness of breath and pronounced eosinophilia, a marked rise in eosinophils in the blood.

The larvae migrate from the intestine to the blood vessels, muscle, heart and brain and form cysts, and encystment in muscle is what causes symptoms.

Occasionally the infection becomes life-threatening: myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle), central nervous system involvement, and pneumonitis (lung inflammation).

A clue to link it with the source: flulike illness with diarrhea, then muscle pain and a high eosinophil count, after eating pork or bear meat.

cards.t: Intestinal roundworms side by side: telling them apart
q: how do I tell the intestinal worms apart
what is the key feature of each intestinal roundworm
cards.x:
A one-line identifier for each intestinal worm:

- Ascaris lumbricoides: eggs swallowed; lung migration with eosinophilic pneumonitis; obstruction with heavy loads.
- Trichuris trichiura (whipworm): eggs swallowed, humans the sole host; localized hemorrhage, dysentery and rectal prolapse.
- Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm): eggs from surroundings, close contact; anal itching; diagnosed by the tape test.
- Hookworms and Strongyloides stercoralis: larvae through the skin; hookworm means blood loss and anemia, while Strongyloides can reinfect the same host.
- Trichinella spiralis: undercooked pork or bear meat; muscle cysts and pronounced eosinophilia.

cards.t: Tissue nematodes (filarial worms): the three to know
q: what are the three filarial worms
cards.x:
Tissue nematodes complete their life cycle in human blood, lymphatics (lymph vessels) or skin. They are the filarial worms: elongate, thread-like worms spread by biting arthropods such as insects. They cause chronic, deforming disease.

The three to know are:

- Wuchereria bancrofti: elephantiasis.
- Onchocerca volvulus: river blindness.
- Loa loa: the eye worm.

All three follow the intermediate-host pattern (cycle D), with the biting insect acting as the intermediate host. Each uses a different insect, which is how to keep them apart: mosquitoes, black flies, and small flies such as mangrove or deer flies.

cards.t: Wuchereria bancrofti and elephantiasis
q: how do people get Wuchereria bancrofti
cards.x:
Wuchereria bancrofti causes bancroftian filariasis, a tropical infection spread by mosquitoes, in this case Anopheles and Culex mosquitoes, found worldwide in the tropics. The mosquito is the intermediate host.

The mosquito deposits larvae when it bites. The larvae move into the lymphatics (the lymph vessels) and develop into adults there.

Chronic infection blocks the lymphatic circulation and causes elephantiasis, massive swelling in the extremities, such as both legs.

cards.t: Onchocerca volvulus and river blindness
cards.x:
Onchocerca volvulus causes river blindness (onchocerciasis). It is transmitted by biting black flies, with the black fly as the intermediate host, in Africa and Latin America.

The larvae develop into adults in the subcutaneous tissues (just under the skin). Adult females migrate through the blood to the eyes and provoke inflammatory reactions there.

The reason for the blindness is a second organism: coinfection with Wolbachia bacteria causes river blindness. These bacteria are an endosymbiont (a microbe that lives inside another organism), and their antigens stimulate an inflammation that damages the cornea, retina and optic nerve.

cards.t: Loa loa (African eye worm)
q: how do people get the African eye worm
cards.x:
Loa loa is the African eye worm. It is spread by the bite of small flies, mangrove flies or deer flies, and it follows the intermediate-host pattern (cycle D).

It is a temperature-sensitive worm that migrates around and under the skin and may enter the eye. Part of its treatment is mechanical: the worm can be pulled from a small hole in the conjunctiva, the clear membrane over the white of the eye, when it shows up there.

cards.t: Filarial worms compared: vector, site and disease
k: mosquito black fly deer fly worms
q: which insect carries each filarial worm
how do the filarial worms differ
cards.x:
The filarial worms are best sorted by vector:

- Wuchereria bancrofti: mosquitoes; lives in the lymphatics; blocked lymph and elephantiasis.
- Onchocerca volvulus: black flies; lives in subcutaneous tissues, and females migrate to the eyes; river blindness, with Wolbachia bacteria.
- Loa loa: small flies (mangrove or deer flies); moves around and under the skin and may enter the eye; the African eye worm.
- Dirofilaria: described as vector-borne, with no vector named; in dogs it causes heartworm, and humans are suboptimal hosts, with the lungs and skin affected.

cards.t: Toxocara canis and cati: humans as accidental hosts
q: what is a paratenic host in Toxocara
cards.x:
Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati are the dog and cat roundworms. Their life cycle is complex, with direct and indirect transmission. Dogs and cats are the definitive hosts, where adults live in the small intestine.

Humans are accidental hosts. A person can be infected by swallowing infective eggs from dog or cat feces. The other route is eating the undercooked meat of a paratenic host (a host in which the organism does not grow, a transport host on the way to the definitive host), such as waterfowl (a duck) or a rabbit.

cards.t: Toxocariasis: ocular and visceral disease
q: what problems does Toxocara cause in humans
cards.x:
In people, the Toxocara larvae migrate through the tissues, and the damage depends on where they go.

- Ocular toxocariasis: the larvae migrate to the eye, which may lead to visual impairment and total blindness.
- Visceral toxocariasis: the larvae cause inflammation and severe damage to the liver.

Link it to the source: dog or cat feces, or the undercooked meat of a transport host, followed by eye or liver damage.

cards.t: Dirofilaria (heartworm) in humans
q: why can Dirofilaria look like lung cancer
what does heartworm do in humans
cards.x:
Dirofilaria is a vector-borne filarial nematode. In dogs it causes heartworm. Humans are suboptimal hosts, meaning the worm does not do well in them, and it shows up in two ways.

- Pulmonary dirofilariasis: the worms produce coin lesions in the lungs that can be mistaken for malignancies (cancers).
- Subcutaneous dirofilariasis: the worms produce nodules, most often in exposed areas of the body.

cards.t: Trematodes (flukes): body plan and hosts
q: who are the hosts of flukes
cards.x:
Trematodes, or flukes, are flatworms with ovoid, leaflike bodies. They have digestive, excretory, neuromuscular and reproductive systems but lack circulatory and respiratory systems.

Animals such as snails or fish are usually the intermediate hosts, and humans are described as the definitive hosts. The sheep liver fluke, Fasciola, is listed with herbivores as its hosts instead.

cards.t: Schistosoma (blood flukes) and schistosomiasis
q: what are the symptoms of schistosomiasis
cards.x:
Schistosoma is the blood fluke. Three species, Schistosoma mansoni, Schistosoma japonicum and the species that lives in the veins of the bladder, cause schistosomiasis, a prominent parasitic disease of Africa, South America, the Middle East and the Far East, affecting 100 million people.

People get it from water where the snail lives: the larva (cercaria) penetrates the skin and moves into the liver to mature. The adults then migrate to the intestine or bladder, feed on blood, and shed eggs into urine and feces.

Symptoms are itchiness at the entry site, fever, chills, diarrhea, cough, and enlargement and inflammation of the liver, spleen and bladder. Prevention is snail control.

cards.t: Schistosoma life cycle and the snail step
q: what is the Schistosoma life cycle
what do miracidia and cercariae do
why are snails needed for Schistosoma
cards.x:
